title: What Gambia Helped the Rohingya Prove in The Hague
author: Parampreet Singh
body:
In early 2019, I was working for Human Rights Watch. A few months earlier, a UN fact-finding mission on Myanmar had concluded that the evidence of atrocities against the Rohingya called for investigating and prosecuting Myanmar military leaders for genocide, crimes against humanity, and war crimes.

At the time, it felt impossibly distant. I approached diplomats in New York and officials in national capitals with an idea: What if a country which is party to the Genocide Convention asked the ICJ to hold Myanmar itself responsible under the treaty? The legal experts were intrigued. The political attachés rolled their eyes. Nobody wanted to touch the idea with a 10-foot pole.

But Abubacarr Tambadou, the Attorney General of Gambia at the time, had found his own compelling reason to act. During a visit to a refugee camp in Bangladesh, he was deeply moved by harrowing testimonies of Rohingya survivors, whose accounts reminded him of atrocities he had encountered as a prosecutor before the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda. His determination to act on what he heard helped set in motion Gambia’s case before the ICJ.

My colleagues and I at Human Rights Watch worked closely with Gambian officials, Rohingya activists, and other civil society groups to advance the effort, both before and after the case was filed. Eleven other countries later intervened in the proceedings to argue how the Genocide Convention should be interpreted.

On Thursday, the International Court of Justice held Myanmar responsible for committing genocide against the Rohingya minority in northern Rakhine state in 2017. The landmark ruling, in a case brought by Gambia, is the first time the Court has found a state directly responsible for violating the 1948 Genocide Convention, and is expected to have significant ramifications for international law and other cases of genocide litigated in the court.

A brief history of Rohingya

The Rohingya, a predominantly Muslim ethnic minority from Myanmar’s Rakhine State, had long lived with limited access to education, healthcare, and freedom of movement. Myanmar labeled them as “illegal immigrants,” carrying out military attacks in the 1970s and 1990s to drive hundreds of thousands of Rohingya into Bangladesh. In 1982, Myanmar passed a citizenship law excluding the Rohingya from a list of ethnic groups formally recognized by the government and effectively denying them citizenship.

In the early 2010s, several bouts of ethnic tensions and violence erupted in Rakhine State and morphed into a “coordinated campaign to forcibly relocate or remove the state’s Muslims,” according to a 2013 Human Rights Watch report. The 2012 attacks brought about a period of increased repression and persecution of Rohingya that laid the groundwork for more brutal military campaigns in 2016 and 2017.

In August and September 2017, Myanmar’s security forces killed thousands of Rohingya men, women, and children in Rakhine State, destroyed hundreds of Rohingya villages, and forced more than 700,000 Rohingya to flee to neighboring Bangladesh.

On Sep. 2, 2017, at the height of the military campaign, Senior General Min Aung Hlaing, the Myanmar army chief, described the Rohingya as a longstanding “problem” and an “unfinished job.” His soldiers openly referred to them as animals and called for violence against them. The military’s campaign of physical destruction was accompanied by a sustained effort to strip the Rohingya of their identity and their very humanity.

What is genocide?

The legal bar to proving the crime of genocide is exceptionally high. On Nov. 11, 2019, Gambia filed a case at the ICJ in The Hague alleging that Myanmar had failed to fulfill its obligations under the Genocide Convention regarding the Rohingya in Rakhine State.

The case hinged on the singular question of intention, which is crucial to defining genocide: Did Myanmar’s security forces commit acts of collective violence against the Rohingya with “intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group, as such.”

In previous cases, the court had ruled that even widespread killings and forced displacement did not necessarily constitute genocide. To establish genocidal intent from a pattern of conduct, it must be the only reasonable conclusion supported by the evidence.

Gambia argued that Myanmar’s atrocities were not simply the excesses of a counterinsurgency campaign, but part of a deliberate effort to destroy the Rohingya as a group. Its case drew on UN investigations, survivor testimony, accounts from former Myanmar soldiers, and satellite imagery documenting mass killings including young children and infants, sexual violence, and the destruction of hundreds of Rohingya villages.

To establish genocidal intent, Gambia pointed to the deliberate targeting of Rohingya civilians, the coordinated nature and extreme brutality of the attacks, the use of sexual violence, decades of discriminatory policies, hate speech by military leaders, and its failure to hold those responsible to account. It argued that these were not isolated atrocities, but part of a sustained campaign against the Rohingya, and that the evidence, taken together, left no reasonable explanation other than an intent to destroy them, at least in part.

Myanmar denied responsibility for its atrocities, portrayed its campaign of “ethnic cleansing” as a counterterrorism operation, and insisted that the violence did not establish an intent to destroy the Rohingya. Lawyers for Myanmar even argued that its security forces had the opportunity to “kill a larger number” of Rohingya if that had been their intent.

On Thursday, the ICJ ruled by nine votes to six that Myanmar had committed genocide against the Rohingya in northern Rakhine state. The court decisively rejected Myanmar’s argument that counterinsurgency alone could explain the conduct of its military and other security forces and affirmed what Rohingya survivors have maintained for years. Its judgment marks a monumental victory for the survivors, whose struggle for justice and a safe return home continues.

The judgment reaffirmed that when genocidal intent is inferred from a pattern of conduct, that intent must be the only reasonable inference from the evidence as a whole. It also clarified that a state can pursue military or security objectives and still act with genocidal intent. The court evaluated evidence from multiple sources, from the findings of UN investigators and experts to witness statements and direct testimonies, to determine whether genocide had occurred.

A victory for international law

The ICJ judgment is particularly important now, as powerful governments increasingly resist scrutiny of their conduct or that of their allies. Some governments are threatening institutions charged with upholding international law and withdrawing their political and financial support. Power politics and selective enforcement have always undermined these institutions, but weakening them further would leave those with the least power even more vulnerable.

Defending these institutions means strengthening ties between governments willing to act on principle and communities fighting for justice. International law made it possible for Gambia, a small West African country, to stand with a persecuted community thousands of miles away and hold another state accountable. Even those with little geopolitical power—small states and marginalized communities alike—can help shape how international law is enforced. Atrocities go unpunished too often, but this ruling shows that impunity is not inevitable.

The case also depended on the courage of Rohingya survivors who shared their experiences with investigators and helped document the military’s atrocities. Some later testified before the court. Civil society activists spent years pressing for international recognition of the Rohingya’s suffering and demanding justice. Many principled diplomats and government officials turned concern into collective action. Through their combined efforts, reports, resolutions, and legal commitments became powerful tools for accountability.

Nearly 1.2 million Rohingya still live as refugees in Bangladesh, hundreds of thousands face discrimination and pushbacks while seeking refuge across the region, and those trapped in Myanmar continue to face persecution and violence. The ICJ has held Myanmar responsible for genocide and ordered it to allow and facilitate the safe, voluntary, and dignified return of the Rohingya displaced by its actions.

Securing its compliance will require the same grit, courage, and solidarity that Rohingya survivors, civil society groups, and governments brought to this case.
